title: Wings in twos and threes
hookLine: He made the angels messengers with wings, two, three and four (35:1)
carry: he adds to creation as he wills

cards: Ask a child to draw an angel, and you'll usually get two wings. White, feathered, one on each side, like a bird's. It's the picture from a thousand paintings and greeting cards.
Surah thirty-five opens with angels too, and in its very first verse it breaks that picture open. Not two wings. Two, or three, or four.
And then a line that suggests the count doesn't stop there. The surah is called Fatir, the Originator, the One who splits creation open from nothing.

teach.b: Verse one praises Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth.
Then, Pickthall: "Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will." Notice the word messengers. In the Qur'an, angels aren't decoration.
They carry things: revelation, mercy, sometimes warning. The Arabic says mathna, wa thulath, wa ruba', in twos, and threes, and fours.

teach.h: HE ADDS TO CREATION AS HE WILLS.
teach.b: Then the open door: yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha', He adds to creation whatever He wills. Many commentators read that as a hint that four isn't a limit. A hadith gives one example.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form with six hundred wings. The verse and the hadith aren't giving an anatomy lesson.
Muslims believe angels are real but unseen, made of light, and that what anyone knows of them comes only from revelation.
The point is humility about the pictures in your head: whatever you imagine, creation is larger, and still being added to. This week ran the same way.

The mothers of the believers, Umm Salamah's question, a blessing that starts with Allah and the angels before it reaches anyone on earth. Mountains singing with Dawud. A termite that knew what the jinn didn't.
A dam that broke when thanks ran dry. Again and again, the world in these surahs is bigger and stranger than the picture you walked in with.

how: Belief in angels is one of the six articles of faith in Islam; Muslims understand them as unseen beings made of light who carry out Allah's commands, known only through the Qur'an and hadith.

o: in twos: the first count of the angels' wings
the wings of birds, as opposed to angels
a pair of angels sent together on a mission

games.q: the opening of Fatir — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an says every angel has two wings
35:1 says two, three and four, and that He adds to creation as He wills.
a hadith says the Prophet saw Jibril with six hundred wings
Ibn Mas'ud reports it in Sahih al-Bukhari.
in the Qur'an, angels are described as messengers

games.q: the verse lists angels' wings: two, three and four. what does it say next?
o: He adds to creation as He wills.
and they never touch the earth.
games.why: He adds to creation whatever He wills, a line many commentators read as saying four isn't a limit.

practice: If you can, step to a window or outside and watch one bird fly: how the wings move, how often, how it turns. If no bird is near, picture the last one you saw.
Then close your eyes with the line, He adds to creation as He wills, and let it widen whatever picture you're holding.

wordCard.voice: Mathna, the word for 'in twos,' opening Surah Fatir's list of the angels' wings: in twos, and threes, and fours. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: in twos, and threes, and fours, the angels' wings in 35:1.

carryVoice: Your line: he adds to creation as he wills. Six hundred wings, in one report. That's the week.

sources.q: Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will.
